extracted.intended_audience: researchers, instructional designers, and educational psychologists interested in cognitive load theory and multimedia instruction
extracted.subtask_description: A synthesis/review of cognitive load theory (CLT) covering instructional effects, empirical findings, measurement techniques, and future research directions relevant to designing and evaluating instruction and learning materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-Management Effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Students can be taught to apply CLT principles themselves to manage their own cognitive load; those taught self-management are hypothesised to deal better with poorly designed materials than students only exposed to CLT-designed materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical study design: three conditions and two phases — (1) split-attention with instruction on self-managing (e.g., reorganising text and diagrams), (2) split-attention without self-management instruction, (3) instructor-managed physically integrated format. The key finding is superior recall and transfer for the self-management group when later presented with split-attention materials in another domain. Implies teaching learners CLT strategies can generalise across domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-Explanation Effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Worked examples combined with self-explanation prompts elicit deeper processing and can be superior to worked examples without prompts, provided total cognitive load remains within working memory capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occurs independently of CLT but explained by it; variability of practice can also stimulate deeper processing when multiple examples are available. If only one example exists, provide self-explanation prompts to elicit sophisticated explanations. Caveat: added germane processing increases total load — benefits only if load stays within capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination Effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Learners asked to imagine or mentally rehearse a concept or process can learn more than learners asked to study equivalent instructional material, but only when learners can adequately imagine the relevant concepts/procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novices may be unable to imagine high element interactivity material due to WM limits, so for novices study instructions may be superior. With increased knowledge, imagining becomes feasible and may surpass study instructions. Example: mentally rehearsing motor tasks; once information can be adequately imagined, imagination instructions are superior (Cooper et al. 2001).

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolated Elements Effect
rubrics_metrics.description: For very high element interactivity information that exceeds working memory, presenting individual elements first (isolated) and later the integrated information can be superior to presenting all information twice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: learners can store individual elements in long-term memory when presented in isolation, then later learn interactions more easily. Similar to simple-to-complex sequencing: start with low element interactivity versions, then progressively more complex tasks (van Merriënboer et al.). Avoid presenting all integrated information repeatedly if WM overload prevents processing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective Working Memory Effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Collaborative learners form a single information-processing system of multiple limited working memories, allowing division of information and a larger effective collective WM, but with transaction costs for communication and coordination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade-off: for tasks imposing high cognitive load, collaborative learning can be more efficient (benefits of distributed processing > transaction costs); for low-load tasks, individual learning is more efficient (transaction costs outweigh benefits). Design implication: use collaborative learning for high intrinsic-load tasks, avoid for low-load tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human Movement Effect
rubrics_metrics.description: For cognitive tasks involving human movement, animation (or observing/making movements) can be more effective than static representations, due to evolved abilities to learn from observing action and mirror-neuron systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Largest effects when animations are highly realistic and procedural-motor knowledge is involved (Höffler & Leutner). Making movements (gestures, tracing) can reduce WM load via cognitive offloading and richer encoding (e.g., tracing angle relationships increased learning). Design: use realistic animations or incorporate gestures/tracing for motor-related instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective Rating Scale (Paas) — specifications and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Paas subjective rating scale provides an overall measure of cognitive load (intrinsic + extraneous) and is sensitive and simple to use, but in its simplicity cannot easily differentiate types of cognitive load.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers have adapted the scale in many ways (different verbal labels like 'task difficulty' vs 'invested mental effort', fewer categories e.g., 5 or 7 instead of 9, single post-task measurement vs averaging multiple measures). Findings: single post-phase measures tend to be higher than averages of multiple during-phase measures (possible WM depletion). Advantages: sensitivity, simplicity; weaknesses: inability to separate load types and issues needing further psychometric research (timing effects, age/gender effects, baseline necessity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiating Types of Cognitive Load via Psychometric Instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Questionnaire-based instruments can be designed to differentiate intrinsic and extraneous cognitive load by using multiple indicators per load type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Leppink et al.'s 10-item psychometric instrument provided support for differentiating intrinsic and extraneous load (2013, 2014). More empirical evidence is needed across domains and with varied questions to confirm robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary Task Techniques for Measuring Cognitive Load
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary task performance (e.g., rhythm method with foot-tapping) is used as an indicator of cognitive load on a primary task, assuming secondary-task performance degrades as primary-task load increases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Park & Brünken's rhythm method sensitive to hypothesised differences. Criticisms: intrusiveness (adds extra cognitive load that may interfere with primary task) and inability to differentiate load types. Use with caution; consider interference and interpretability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological Techniques for Measuring Cognitive Load
rubrics_metrics.description: Physiological measures (EEG, fMRI, eye-tracking variables like pupil dilation, blink rate, fixation time, saccades) provide objective correlates of cognitive load.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EEG has reflected hypothesised load differences in hypertext learning studies; pupil dilation correlates with cognitive load in young but not old adults. Mobile measuring devices facilitate use, but more research is needed into validity, age effects, domain-general applicability, and whether measures differentiate load types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working Memory Resource Depletion Hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Working memory resources can become depleted after sustained cognitive exertion, reducing capacity to commit further resources; WM capacity may be variable rather than fixed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implications: may explain spacing effects (massed practice reduces WM capacity compared to spaced practice). If confirmed, CLT's assumption that long-term memory content is the only major determinant of WM characteristics must be revised; instructional design should account for depletion (spacing, breaks). Evidence: Chen et al. (2018) data suggest massed presentations reduce WM capacity relative to spaced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive Load Theory and Self-Regulated Learning (task involvement & regulation accuracy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine CLT with self-regulated learning constructs: task involvement (high performance + high invested effort) and regulation accuracy (selection of suitable tasks based on performance and invested effort).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures: task selection behavior, judgements of learning, allocation of study time, restudy decisions, and performance combined to assess regulation. Learners often use invalid cues (ease of processing) — cue-utilisation framework (Koriat) proposed to teach use of more valid cues (e.g., generate keywords after delay, explain solutions to peers). Evidence for teachable, domain-general self-regulation improving far transfer is currently limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotions, Stress, and Uncertainty as Environmental Factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical learning environment factors (cognitive: uncertainty; physiological: stress; affective: emotions) can restrict WM by competing with task-relevant processes, increasing cognitive load and hampering learning and transfer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design implication depends on whether these are treated as extraneous (to be reduced) or intrinsic (part of task to be trained). For vocational/professional tasks, training should include emotions/stress/uncertainty so learners develop competencies to perform under such states. Possible interventions: imagination/mental practice before tasks, collaboration to use collective WM for novices; consider whether stress/emotion should be simulated rather than prevented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human Movement as an Additional Modality in Working Memory Models
rubrics_metrics.description: Motor information (gestures, tracing, making movements) can affect available WM resources and cognitive load — sometimes reducing WM load by offloading and richer encoding — suggesting human movement may be an additional modality to consider in WM models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: gestures/tracing can improve problem solving and transfer (e.g., tracing angle relationships; iPad tracing of graphs). Theoretical implication: existing WM models may need to incorporate motor/embodied modalities (integrated distributed attention model proposed). Instructional implication: incorporate gestures/tracing for certain tasks, but be cautious because motor info can also occupy WM.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compound Effects and Expertise-Dependent Design Principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Compound effects indicate limits of other cognitive load effects and highlight that optimal instructional design principles depend on learner expertise and stage of training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: four-component instructional design (4C/ID) uses compound effects to select design principles across curriculum stages — as learners grow expertise, previously optimal principles may change. Instructional designers should consider how effects interact and vary with learner knowledge when selecting techniques (e.g., worked examples, variability, isolation).
